bibliography.abstract: Civilian drones have rapidly expanded from niche technologies to widespread tools for recreation and commerce, yet their diffusion remains uneven. This study analyzes the U.S. drone registration data (2016–2019) to examine how digital infrastructure and regulation shape adoption patterns. After data cleaning and county-level aggregation, broadband access, built environment, and state policy interventions were tested as predictors using an integrated framework of spatial–temporal hotspot analysis and Multiscale Geographically Weighted Regression (MGWR). While global OLS results identify broadband connectivity as a primary correlate, the MGWR analysis reveals significant spatial non-stationarity, indicating that the associations of broadband and housing density with adoption vary across regions. Specifically, digital infrastructure exhibits a stronger positive association with adoption in rural and developing regions compared to established tech hubs. Adoption clusters in urban and affluent areas, revealing persistent digital and social divides. These findings highlight how infrastructure and governance are jointly associated with the spread of emerging technologies through spatially distinct mechanisms, underscoring the need for adaptive, place-based policy frameworks in the drone era.

en.caveats: The analysis relies on county-level aggregations of registration data, which may mask finer-grained neighborhood-level disparities in drone adoption.
en.what: This study analyzed U.S. county-level drone registration data from 2016 to 2019 using spatial-temporal hotspot analysis and Multiscale Geographically Weighted Regression (MGWR) to identify predictors of civilian drone adoption. While global models identify broadband access as the primary correlate, the MGWR model reveals that the positive association of digital infrastructure with drone adoption is stronger in rural and developing regions than in established technology hubs.
en.why: It demonstrates that the adoption of physical-digital technologies like drones does not spread uniformly, showing that local digital infrastructure and housing density act as spatially distinct drivers that can exacerbate existing urban-rural and socioeconomic divides.
